strengths: Large-scale pretraining experiments (3B on 250B tokens, 8B on 1T tokens, multiple seeds) are rare in the literature and lend credibility to the empirical claims; the breadth of baselines (NTP, MTP, DS-MTP, MTP-Skip variants, handcrafted summaries) and ablations (tf-idf reweighting, summary window length, RevLM layer depth) is commendable.

The paper offers a clear conceptual framing: replacing multiple token-prediction auxiliary heads with a single head that predicts a compact summary of the long-term future, with an informative analysis on synthetic benchmarks (path-star and modified sibling discovery) that separates 'long-horizon supervision' from 'adaptive/filtered supervision' and motivates the learned-summary variant.

The two-tier methodology (handcrafted bag-of-words BCE summaries and learned RevLM-distilled summaries) is sensible, and the synthetic studies (Figure 3, Figure 4, Table 4) provide mechanistic insight into when each variant helps, rather than only reporting aggregate benchmark gains.

Related work coverage is thorough (MTP variants, TRELAWNEY, BST, Meet-in-the-Middle), and the paper is honest about design choices such as constraining MTP to a single auxiliary head for a consistent comparison.
weaknesses: The iso-compute comparison is not fair for the main method: FSP-RevLM requires training a full reverse LM (same size as the forward model) on the same data, effectively doubling the pretraining compute, yet the paper explicitly excludes this from the compute budget. For pretraining objectives, this is a central concern—many of the claimed gains over NTP/MTP could plausibly be recovered by simply training the baseline longer, and no iso-compute experiment (e.g., NTP trained with 2x tokens, or distillation from a forward teacher) is provided to rule this out.

The headline results are weaker and less consistent than claimed. At 3B scale, DS-MTP beats FSP-RevLM on most tasks (ARC-Easy/Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+); at 8B, NTP still wins on GSM8K. The 'up to 5%' figure comes largely from ARC-Easy, a knowledge/recall benchmark that does not obviously test the long-horizon reasoning/planning the paper's motivation centers on.

Evaluation procedure risks inflating results: pass@k scores are computed by sweeping temperatures (0 to 1.0) and reporting the best temperature per method and per task on the test benchmarks, a form of test-set selection that is not standard and is not clearly justified.

Several statistically fragile results: many 8B differences (e.g., MATH 0.351±0.017 vs NTP 0.342±0.008; MBPP 0.683 vs DS-MTP 0.678) overlap within standard errors over 3 seeds, yet are narrated as meaningful improvements.

The motivation (creative writing, narrative coherence, long-horizon planning) is not matched by the evaluation; no long-form generation, document-level coherence, or planning benchmarks are used, so the central mechanism (reduced teacher forcing for long-form generation) is not directly validated at scale.

The learned-summary objective is heuristic and under-specified theoretically: why is regressing onto the RevLM hidden state (which predicts the previous token from the suffix) the right target, and what information is provably retained or discarded? The ℓ2 matching loss also lacks discussion of representation alignment issues between independently trained models.

Novelty is moderate: the components (reverse/bidirectional training à la BST and Meet-in-the-Middle, distillation to an auxiliary head, lookahead objectives à la TRELAWNEY) are individually established; the contribution is mostly their combination plus scale, and the distinction from BST/MiM is more about objective engineering than a new capability.

Presentation issues: several typos ('radomly', 'reverseLM'), inconsistent citation of Gemma technical reports, and claims in the abstract ('creative writing') that outrun the evidence; appendix ablation conclusions (e.g., tf-idf helps 'in most cases' with listed exceptions) are somewhat ad hoc and could benefit from clearer criteria for design decisions.

strengths: Large-scale evaluation is a genuine strength: pretraining 3B and 8B models (250B/1T tokens) across multiple objectives is expensive and rarely done in academic settings, giving the claims more credibility than typical small-scale studies.

The paper includes a thoughtful set of comparisons (NTP, MTP, DS-MTP, MTP-Skip variants, FSP-BCE at multiple window sizes, FSP-RevLM) plus ablations (tf-idf reweighting, RevLM layer depth, number of auxiliary heads).

The synthetic-task analysis (path-star, modified sibling discovery) is well-motivated and provides conceptual clarity about when hand-crafted vs. learned summaries should help, connecting nicely to the 'Clever Hans'/shortcut literature.

The auxiliary-head architecture is simple and cleanly presented (Figure 2), and the idea of compressing long-horizon future information into a single summary target is intuitive and easy to implement.
weaknesses: Questionable experimental fairness: FSP-RevLM requires training an entire additional reverse language model (same architecture, same data) as a teacher. The paper explicitly excludes this cost from the comparison ('Note' in Sec. 4.1), arguing it is a 'one-time overhead' to be amortized. This is not standard for pretraining objectives—an iso-compute comparison is the accepted norm, and under a fair accounting FSP-RevLM uses roughly 2x the compute of all baselines. The reported gains (1–3 points) could plausibly be explained by the extra compute/capacity alone.

The MTP and DS-MTP baselines appear handicapped: both are restricted to a single auxiliary head predicting only the immediate next token. The paper's own Table 4 shows more auxiliary heads materially help MTP. Deployed systems (DeepSeek-V3) use multiple heads; comparing against this weakened configuration inflates the apparent advantage of FSP.

Results are mixed and modest, which contradicts the framing: at 3B scale, DS-MTP beats FSP-RevLM on most tasks; at 8B, vanilla NTP still wins on GSM8K; HumanEval+ ties with MTP. The abstract's claim of 'gains of up to 5%' cherry-picks the best case (ARC-Easy), and ARC improvements coexist with suspicious DS-MTP numbers (0.617 ARC-Easy at 8B vs. 0.736 for MTP), which warrants explanation.

Evaluation methodology concerns: pass@k is reported at the temperature selected to maximize performance for each method and task—effectively test-set selection that can bias comparisons, particularly with only 3 seeds and standard errors that often overlap (e.g., MATH 0.351 ± 0.017 vs. 0.342 ± 0.008). No significance testing is provided.

Limited novelty: distilling reverse-model representations into a forward LM closely echoes Belief State Transformers, Meet-in-the-Middle, and reverse/lookahead objectives (Thankaraj et al., 2025); the bag-of-future-tokens variant is a straightforward multi-label auxiliary loss. The framing as a new pretraining paradigm overstates the incremental conceptual step.

Missing standard evidence: no perplexity/loss curves, no iso-FLOP comparison, no analysis of auxiliary-loss weight sensitivity, and no demonstration on long-form generation quality—the very capability (long-horizon coherence, narrative/creative writing) used to motivate the work is never evaluated. The choice of window τ and where the summary is anchored (t+2 onward) is not ablated on real data.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: typos ('radomly'), inconsistent figure labeling, and the 3B ARC-Easy scores (~0.26–0.29) being dramatically lower than 8B (~0.72–0.77) with no discussion suggest possible evaluation configuration differences that are not addressed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine limitation of multi-token prediction (short-horizon auxiliary heads, impractical scaling of auxiliary heads) and proposes a sensible alternative—predicting a compact summary of the long-term future rather than individual future tokens.
Two complementary instantiations (handcrafted multi-hot FSP-BCE and learned FSP-RevLM) with an honest comparison between them, rather than only championing the more complex variant.

Rare large-scale pretraining evidence: 3B and 8B models trained on 250B/1T tokens with multiple seeds and standard error reporting, comparing against NTP, MTP, and DeepSeek-MTP—a breadth of comparison that is uncommon at this scale.

Good mechanistic analysis via synthetic tasks (path-star, modified sibling discovery) that cleanly disentangles when long-range summaries help (path-star) versus when adaptive/learned summaries are needed (sibling discovery), with supporting ablations on auxiliary head counts (Table 4) and tf-idf reweighting and reverse-LM layer depth (Table 5).

Overall consistent positive story at 8B scale: FSP-RevLM is best or tied on most benchmarks, with particularly meaningful gains on MATH and ARC-Easy, and the FSP-BCE results (Table 3) helpfully show that the benefit comes from the summary target rather than just the auxiliary head.
weaknesses: Mixed results at 3B scale: DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on the majority of tasks (ARC-Easy/Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+), and the claimed scaling advantage (3B to 8B) is supported by only two scale points; the narrative of 'gains up to 5%' is stronger than what Tables 1–2 uniformly support.

Unfavorable compute accounting for the headline method: FSP-RevLM requires training a full reverse language model (roughly doubling pretraining compute), yet iso-compute comparisons are explicitly excluded via a distillation-style argument. An iso-compute baseline (e.g., NTP/MTP trained with ~2x tokens) or DS-MTP variants is needed to substantiate that the gains come from the objective and not from the extra compute.

DS-MTP at 8B performs anomalously poorly (ARC-Easy 0.617 vs ~0.72–0.77 for all others), which weakens the credibility of the baseline setup; without diagnosis of why, the comparison may be misleading.

Evaluation methodology concerns: pass@k is computed by sweeping 11 temperature values and reporting the best per method and per task, which inflates scores differentially across methods and complicates comparability; GSM8K at 8B actually regresses under FSP-RevLM relative to NTP (0.705 vs 0.716), which is glossed over.

Benchmark coverage is relatively narrow (six benchmarks, no perplexity/loss curves, no long-context or long-form generation evaluation despite the core claims about long-horizon generation quality, narrative coherence, and planning); the abstract's claims about 'creative writing' and 'long-form generations' are not directly evaluated.

Conceptual novelty is moderate: distilling information from a reverse/bidirectional model into a forward LM is closely related to Meet-in-the-Middle (Nguyen et al., 2023) and the Belief State Transformer (Hu et al., 2024); the positioning discussion is reasonable but the delta over MiM is essentially 'distillation instead of parameter sharing,' which deserves more direct empirical comparison against MiM/BST-style baselines rather than discussion alone.

Several design choices appear under-justified: why predictions start at xt+2 (skipping xt+1), how the RevLM summary dimension is chosen, sensitivity of the ℓ2-matching loss weight, and why DS-MTP is excluded from the Table 3 analysis; the effect of the auxiliary loss weight on the main NTP objective is not studied.

Some typographical/clarity issues ('radomly sampling', 'figure 4'), and the teacher-forcing reduction argument ('Why Future Summary Prediction?') is intuitive but not formalized or directly measured, so the causal explanation for the gains remains speculative.

strengths: Rare large-scale pretraining evaluation: 3B and 8B models trained on 250B/1T tokens with three seeds and standard errors, and a breadth of baselines (NTP, MTP, DS-MTP) plus contributed summary variants (MTP-Skip, FSP-BoW) that isolates the effect of different auxiliary targets.

The synthetic analyses (path-star and modified sibling discovery) are well-designed and provide genuine conceptual insight: they cleanly demonstrate when long-range handcrafted summaries help (path-star, Table 4 showing MTP fails even with 4 aux heads) and when they fail (sibling discovery), motivating the learned-summary variant.

The FSP-BoW vs FSP-RevLM distinction is informative and the ablations (tf-idf reweighting, layer depth of RevLM targets, data-constrained regimes at both scales, LM-metric sanity checks in Appendix D.2/D.4) are thorough and transparent.
Data-constrained experiments (Figure 6, Figure 8, 20-50 epoch regimes) are timely and support a useful practical narrative that future-aware objectives extract more signal per unique token.

Honest and detailed related-work discussion that carefully positions the work against Twin Networks, SemFormer, BST, MiM, and ProphetNet, and the paper is generally well written and clearly organized.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not compute-fair: FSP-RevLM roughly doubles training FLOPs (same-size reverse LM trained for the same number of steps), yet is compared at iso-data only against NTP/MTP baselines trained on a single forward pass. The authors explicitly exclude the teacher's cost, citing distillation practice, but unlike standard distillation the teacher here is a full extra pretraining run; an iso-compute NTP baseline (2x tokens) or a smaller forward model could plausibly close the 2-5 point gains. This weakens the headline claim that FSP is a better pretraining objective per unit of compute.

Results are inconsistent across scales: at 3B (Table 2), DS-MTP beats FSP-RevLM on most tasks (ARC-Easy 0.293 vs 0.277, ARC-Challenge 0.274 vs 0.255, MBPP 0.537 vs 0.524, HumanEval+ 0.348 vs 0.305), and at 8B NTP still leads on GSM8K (0.716 vs 0.705). The claim of general superiority rests mainly on 8B results obtained with double the compute.

Some reported numbers are questionable: ARC results show zero standard error over 3 seeds (e.g., 0.766 (0.000), and the large MTP-Skip tau:32 ARC-Challenge drop to 0.379 with 0.000 SE), which is implausible for pass@1 across independently seeded pretraining runs and suggests possible evaluation/procedural issues. Additionally, pass@k with per-method temperature selection is a form of test-set tuning, and pass@16 is a weak metric for base models without post-training.

The main baseline is constrained: both MTP and DS-MTP are limited to a single auxiliary head, while the practical motivation of MTP (and its use in DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-3) involves multi-head variants; the iso-head comparison is internally consistent but weakens the 'Beyond Multi-Token Prediction' framing, and no comparison against multi-head MTP, TRELAWNEY, or L-MTP-style baselines is included despite these being directly discussed.

Novelty is moderate: the BoW variant closely mirrors prior set-level future-supervision objectives (Yin et al., 2024; Frydenlund, 2025), and the learned-summary variant is essentially Twin Networks (2017) scaled to transformers; the contribution is best viewed as an empirical scaling study of known ideas rather than a fundamentally new objective.

No evaluation after SFT/post-training or on long-form generation quality (narrative coherence, planning), which are the tasks the motivation (exposure bias, teacher forcing) explicitly targets; downstream gains are confined to a narrow set of pass@k benchmark numbers, and the claimed link to improved RL fine-tunability (via diversity in Figure 5) is only conjecture.

Auxiliary loss weighting and the lambda between NTP and summary losses (Eq. 7) are not ablated in the main text, and the 'Why FSP reduces teacher forcing' argument is conceptual rather than measured (e.g., no direct quantification of teacher-forcing reduction or of what information the summaries retain).

strengths: Rare breadth of large-scale experimentation: pretraining runs at 3B and 8B scale on 250B/1T tokens, with six pretraining objectives compared under iso-data conditions across multiple benchmarks, plus a data-constrained (multi-epoch) analysis that is increasingly relevant.

The paper is honest about compute caveats and explicitly discusses the doubled cost of FSP-RevLM and the iso-data vs. iso-compute distinction, which is more transparent than much of the MTP literature.

The synthetic-task analysis (path-star, sibling discovery) provides a useful conceptual lens for when handcrafted long-horizon summaries help and when they add noise, and the narrative of moving from handcrafted to learned summaries is coherent.
Includes sensible ablations (number of auxiliary heads, tf-idf reweighting, RevLM depth, summary windows) and language-modeling sanity checks in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core fairness of the headline comparisons is questionable: FSP-RevLM trains a same-size reverse model for the same number of steps, roughly doubling training FLOPs versus all baselines, yet the main tables are iso-data rather than iso-compute. The authors' justification (compute-rich, data-limited regime) is asserted rather than demonstrated; an iso-compute NTP baseline (2x tokens or a larger model) is missing and could plausibly erase most gains.

Novelty is limited. The authors themselves acknowledge that bag-of-words future summaries closely resemble SemFormer (Yin et al., 2024) and Frydenlund (2025), and that aligning forward states with a reverse model is essentially Twin Networks (Serdyuk et al., 2017) transplanted to transformers. The unifying 'FSP framework' framing is largely presentational; the genuinely new element (RevLM distillation at scale) is a straightforward combination of known ideas.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent with the paper's claims. At 8B, FSP-RevLM loses to vanilla NTP on GSM8K and only ties MTP on HumanEval+; at 3B, DS-MTP is better than FSP-RevLM on most tasks. The abstract's framing of improvements 'across math, reasoning, and coding benchmarks' overstates what the tables show, and 'up to 5%' gains cherry-picks the best cases. Differences are often within ~1-3 points with 3 seeds and no significance testing.

The teacher-forcing motivation is conceptually shaky: the auxiliary targets are still derived entirely from ground-truth future tokens, so the method does not actually reduce exposure bias in the classic sense. The claim that predicting summaries 'substantially reduces teacher forcing' is asserted without measurement.

Evaluation methodology has weaknesses: pass@k is reported at the temperature that maximizes pass@k per method and task (selection on the test set), code/math results use pass@16 rather than pass@1, and with only 3 seeds many reported improvements are within one standard error.

Comparison baselines are constrained in a way that favors the proposed method: both MTP and DS-MTP are limited to a single auxiliary head predicting the immediate next token, whereas the standard MTP configurations that demonstrated success at scale (e.g., DeepSeek-V3 with multiple heads) are not directly compared at full strength; the multi-head ablation appears only in the small-scale synthetic setting.

Reproducibility is limited: the pretraining corpus is described only loosely ('DCLM-like sources'), no code or model release is mentioned, and some details (e.g., auxiliary loss weighting, RevLM layer choice rationale) are scattered or only briefly justified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: what auxiliary pretraining objectives can extract more signal from fixed data, and it proposes a clean, unified 'future summary prediction' framing that subsumes MTP variants and clarifies trade-offs between hand-crafted and learned future targets.

Rare experimental scale and breadth: 3B and 8B parameter pretraining runs (250B/1T tokens), three random seeds, multiple MTP variants (MTP, DS-MTP, MTP-Skip, FSP-BoW, FSP-RevLM), with detailed architecture and hyperparameter documentation that supports reproducibility.

The synthetic analysis (path-star and modified sibling discovery) is well designed: it demonstrates empirically why long summaries matter (path-star) and why *adaptive* summaries matter (sibling discovery), which is more insightful than simply reporting benchmark deltas.

The data-constrained pretraining analysis (Figure 6, Figure 8, Appendix D.4) is a valuable addition showing that future-aware objectives degrade more gracefully than NTP under repeated data, connecting to an active research thread.
The related work is unusually thorough (Appendix A/B), honestly situating the method relative to Twin Networks, SemFormer, MiM, BST, and ProphetNet.
weaknesses: Unfavorable compute accounting for the headline method: FSP-RevLM trains a reverse model of the same size for the same number of steps, roughly doubling training compute versus NTP/MTP. The main tables (Tables 1-2) are therefore iso-data but not iso-compute, and it is unclear how much of the reported gain over MTP/NTP is simply due to extra compute. The paper's justification (data-wall argument) is asserted rather than demonstrated; an iso-compute baseline (e.g., NTP trained 2x longer, or a 2x-width NTP model) is missing.

Evidence for the central claim is mixed and inconsistent across scales: at 3B, DS-MTP beats FSP-RevLM on most tasks (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+); at 8B, NTP beats FSP-RevLM on GSM8K and FSP only ties MTP on HumanEval+. The 'up to 5% gains' narrative overstates what is a collection of small, task-dependent improvements with overlapping standard errors in several cases.

A serious evaluation-methodology concern: pass@k is computed by sweeping decoding temperatures (0 to 1.0) and reporting the best temperature per method per task. Without a held-out validation split for this selection, this adaptive tuning on evaluation benchmarks can inflate and bias comparisons, especially given that several reported differences are within ~1 standard error.

Limited novelty over prior work: FSP-BoW closely mirrors unordered set-level future-token prediction objectives (Yin et al. 2024; Frydenlund 2025), and FSP-RevLM is essentially Twin Networks (Serdyuk et al. 2017) transplanted to transformer pretraining; the contribution is primarily a careful empirical synthesis rather than a fundamentally new objective.

The theoretical framing around 'reduced teacher forcing' is informal and never operationalized; the paper motivates long-horizon reasoning, planning, and creative writing, but evaluates on only six short-context benchmarks with no long-form generation, narrative coherence, or planning evaluations that would directly test the claimed mechanism. Language-modeling deltas (Tables 6-7) are near zero, which is consistent with the auxiliary signal mostly acting as a mild regularizer.

Design choices appear tuned on the downstream evaluation sets (choice of tf-idf reweighting, last-layer summary, kept only if they helped on specific benchmarks in D.3), further weakening confidence in generalization of the reported gains.
